history: Take any number of bodies and give each a charge equal to $G^{1/2}$ times its mass. Newton's attraction and Coulomb's repulsion then cancel between every pair, at every distance, so the bodies stay wherever they are put [hartle1972]. The same truce holds in general relativity, where Sudhansu Datta Majumdar and Achilles Papapetrou's static solutions of 1947 keep such bodies at rest in any arrangement [majumdar1947, papapetrou1947, hartle1972]. Does the truce survive if the bodies spin?¶Zoltán Perjés answered yes from the Central Research Institute for Physics in Budapest, in a letter received on 8 November 1971 and printed on 13 December [perjes1971]. He had exact solutions "characterized by a flat 'background' three-space", and he read them as the fields "of one or more spinning sources with unit specific charge in stationary configuration" [perjes1971]. Werner Israel and Gordon Wilson generated the same fields from solutions of Laplace's equation, "a stationary generalization of the static electromagnetic vacuum fields of Weyl, Majumdar, and Papapetrou", printed in June 1972 [israel1972, kallosh1994iwp]. Israel had shared the work before then with James Hartle and Stephen Hawking, who thanked him, in a paper received on 10 January 1972, for "communicating his results in advance of publication" [hartle1972].¶Majumdar and Papapetrou's recipe takes a real solution $U$ of Laplace's equation in flat space, the potential of a set of point charges, and Israel and Wilson's lets $U$ be complex [hartle1972]. The metric is $$ds^2 = -|U|^{-2}\left(c\,dt + \vec{\omega}\cdot d\mathbf{x}\right)^2 + |U|^2\,d\mathbf{x}\cdot d\mathbf{x},$$ where the curl of the vector $\vec{\omega}$ is fixed by $U$ and vanishes when $U$ is real [hartle1972]. The electric potential and a magnetic potential are the real and imaginary parts of $1/U$ [hartle1972]. Laplace's equation is linear, so the potentials of many sources add up to one $U$, as they do for Majumdar and Papapetrou [hartle1972].¶What does a complex $U$ describe? Take one point source, $U = 1 + m/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0|$, and move it to an imaginary place, $\mathbf{x}_0 = (0, 0, ia)$: Israel and Wilson found Kerr and Newman's spinning charged body, with its charge equal to its mass and $a$ its angular momentum per unit mass [hartle1972, newman1965kn, kallosh1994iwp]. Give the source a complex mass, $U = 1 + (M + iN)/r$, and the field is Dieter Brill's charged NUT space of 1964, regular outside $r = 0$ only if time is periodic, as in Charles Misner's treatment of NUT space [hartle1972, brill1964, misner1963]. Two sources with imaginary parts $N$ and $-N$, a distance $a$ apart, make an asymptotically flat field of angular momentum $Na$, with $\vec{\omega}$ singular on the axis between them [hartle1972]. By 1973 Leonard Parker, Remo Ruffini, and Daniel Wilkins had the explicit metric of two identical Kerr-Newman sources "in equilibrium under their mutual electromagnetic and gravitational forces, with their spins oppositely oriented along a given axis" [parker1973].¶Hartle and Hawking went through these fields looking for black holes and came back with only the static ones [hartle1972]. The Kerr-Newman member "has a naked singularity and no horizons", since a spinning charged body keeps a horizon only while $Q^2 \le M^2 - a^2$, and with $Q^2 = M^2$ that means $a = 0$ [hartle1972, kallosh1994iwp]. For a space that is flat far away, with the usual topology there, they concluded that "there are no black hole Israel-Wilson metrics" [hartle1972]. They conjectured that Majumdar and Papapetrou's static holes are the only stationary solutions with more than one black hole and no naked singularity [hartle1972]. A proof under certain conditions came in 2006 from Piotr Chruściel, Harvey Reall, and Paul Tod: a regular black hole of the class belongs to Majumdar and Papapetrou's family [chrusciel2006].¶Why should mass equal charge so exactly? Gary Gibbons and Christopher Hull showed in 1982 that the mass of a spacetime is bounded below by its electric and magnetic charges, "the analogue of the Bogomolny bound for magnetic monopoles", and the bound is attained only by fields that are locally of Israel, Wilson, and Perjés's form [gibbons1982, chrusciel2006]. In 1983 Tod found every metric that admits a supercovariantly constant spinor in Gibbons and Hull's sense: this class, with charged dust allowed as a source, and plane waves [tod1983, chrusciel2006]. So the spinning members count as supersymmetric ground states of $N = 2$ supergravity, naked singularities and all, a result Renata Kallosh, David Kastor, Tomás Ortín, and Tibor Torma called "troubling" in June 1994 [kallosh1994iwp]. Kallosh and Ortín had argued in April 1994 that the trace anomaly of $N = 2$ supergravity breaks the supersymmetry of the Kerr-Newman members [kallosh1994anomaly]. The four authors then found fields of the same kind in gravity with a dilaton and an axion, which embeds in $N = 4$ supergravity, where the anomaly vanishes and the supersymmetry holds [kallosh1994iwp].

related.text: The same balanced charges at rest. A real $U$ has $\vec{\omega} = 0$, and the metric is Majumdar and Papapetrou's [hartle1972].

One source at an imaginary place is Kerr and Newman's metric with charge equal to mass, in the radius $r + m$ [hartle1972]. With that much charge any spin leaves the ring singularity naked [kallosh1994iwp].

One source of complex mass is NUT space with a charge added, Brill's solution with charge radius $\sqrt{m^2 + l^2}$ [hartle1972, brill1964]. It keeps the singular axis of NUT space, which Misner's periodic time removes [misner1963].

Tod's other class. A spacetime with a supercovariantly constant spinor is one of Israel, Wilson, and Perjés's fields where the spinor's Killing vector is timelike, and a pp-wave where it is null everywhere [tod1983, chrusciel2006].
